chunks.content: ## Overview of Sound Transition and Shoulder Segmentation This section explains the process of introducing a sound transition with a division line during shoulder segmentation. Key terms include division line, shoulder line, sound transition, folds, and throat shapes. When comparing the style to the original shape, certain sounds such as the A sound and the Xionglong sound disappear, transferring their influence onto the division line, which coincides with the shoulder. This transfer causes folds to appear along the division line. The B sound also disappears and must be eliminated from the design. A division line that does not pass through any sound should be drawn first. An internal line can be added to the shoulder line by right-clicking on it and selecting the option to add an internal shoulder line. The size of this internal line (e.g., 40 or 45) is adjusted based on the style to achieve balance. The balanced choice is preferred for the best fit. --- ## Procedure for Removing B-Throat and Adjusting Shoulder Lines This section details the steps for removing the B-throat and transferring the A-throat to the shoulder line, including rotation and adjustment techniques. When a division line is present but does not pass through sound, the affected piece of material is first cut out. The B-throat is removed initially, followed by transferring the A-throat to the shoulder line. This often results in many wrinkles on one side. There are two approaches to B-throat removal: removing first or not removing first. Removal is more suitable for joints with a broken waistline since unequal lines prevent rotation. To adjust, set a specific value such as 118.3 on the line, ensuring the B-point direction points outward and cannot be moved. Select two edges with a right-click, then rotate the shoulder line starting from the division line with the middle point at the B-point. Rotate the shoulder line minimally, moving it upward rather than shaping the throat. The lower throat is removed next. Holding Shift, select the two edges of the A-throat and rotate the throat from the division line to the B-point. If a small hole remains, push the B-point directly to the top, ensuring the shoulder line transfers to the division line. --- ## Handling Fold Angles and Smoothing Techniques This section covers the treatment of folds, especially broken folds, and the smoothing process using editing tools. If the division line is a fold, the angle may be acceptable. However, if it is a broken fold, it must be adjusted to a smooth curve. This involves deleting the problematic section and using an editor to smooth the line. During this adjustment, remove unnecessary parts such as the front center line and broken lines. Delete segments that are not required to maintain a clean pattern. --- ## Border Line Manipulation and Sealing Process This section describes how to manage border lines, open borders, sealing side seams, and reducing line complexity to improve the pattern's quality.

chunks.content: However, if it is a broken fold, it must be adjusted to a smooth curve. This involves deleting the problematic section and using an editor to smooth the line. During this adjustment, remove unnecessary parts such as the front center line and broken lines. Delete segments that are not required to maintain a clean pattern. --- ## Border Line Manipulation and Sealing Process This section describes how to manage border lines, open borders, sealing side seams, and reducing line complexity to improve the pattern's quality. Select the front center line, then right-click and choose the opposite option to open the border line. After opening, seal the side seams by selecting the lines and applying the seal function. Because sound transitions carry over previous sound edges, these edges must be sealed properly. Remove sealed lines that are redundant. Points can be converted into free-line points to reduce complexity—only retain points essential for structural integrity. Make the waistline smooth by selecting points within a frame and converting them into free-line points. --- ## Dividing Border Lines and Final Rounding This section explains dividing border lines on the shoulder and front lines and rounding off the entire piece for better 3D simulation. Divide the shoulder border line and the front line by pressing the shift key and applying the divide function. After dividing, round off the entire piece to improve the 3D effect and ensure smoothness. Check the border lines for faults before simulation. If no faults are detected, proceed with simulation. --- ## Managing Line Elasticity to Prevent Distortion This section addresses how to prevent distortion when long and short lines interact by adjusting line elasticity. When a long line and a short line are interlocked, the short line tends to be pulled out of shape. To avoid this, enable elasticity on the short border line and set its proportion to 100%. This adjustment stabilizes the short line, preventing deformation. --- ## Quality Improvement for Natural and Smooth Effects This section discusses quality considerations for achieving more natural and smooth shoulder segmentation effects. If high-quality materials or designs are unavailable, the naturalness and smoothness of the effect, especially with fewer voice twists, can be improved by enhancing the quality of the pattern. --- ## Final Observations on Shoulder Shape and Style Matching This section summarizes the final comparison between the adjusted shoulder shape and the original style reference. The side bulge closely resembles the round shape in the style reference but differs slightly in shape. The throat's position shifts to the shoulder, and the shape transforms from a throat to a fold. These adjustments provide a solid base for the final shoulder shape. --- # Summary This document outlines the detailed technical process of provincial transfer with shoulder segmentation, focusing on sound transition management, throat removal, shoulder line adjustment, fold smoothing, border line handling, elasticity settings, and quality improvements to align with style references.
